Chapter 2: Finding a Voice in Law, Activism, and Partnership
Stepping into law school? Well, it honestly felt like landing in a whole new universe. Picture this: classrooms buzzing with sharp minds, strong opinions everywhere, and competition that never let up.
For a woman in the early seventies, the pressure was even heavier. There were only a handful of women in each class, and the message was loud and clear—prove you deserve to be here, or risk getting pushed aside.
It was daunting, no doubt. But that challenge? It sparked a quiet determination. She found herself pulled toward issues that really mattered—children’s rights, access to education, the law’s power to actually protect people who needed it most.
Now, outside those classrooms, the world wasn’t exactly calm either. The Vietnam War was still raging, and the fight for civil rights was far from over. She and her classmates dove into legal aid clinics, working with people who honestly had nowhere else to turn. That’s when the law stopped being just words on a page—it became something urgent, something real.
It was clear: law could be a tool for justice, but only if the people using it actually cared enough to fight for what’s right.
During those years, she met someone—a fellow student whose curiosity and ambition matched hers. He was from another part of the country, had his own style, and a serious passion for politics. What started as friendship grew into something more, built on shared values and a real sense of possibility.
The idea of partnership—of building a life together while chasing separate dreams—began to take shape. It definitely wasn’t always easy. There were those long, late-night talks about the future, about where to live and how to juggle ambition and commitment. But the connection was real, and it brought both comfort and challenge.
After graduation, she faced a big decision: take the traditional route with a big-city law firm, or risk everything and move somewhere she could make a real, direct impact. Heading south, to a place with deep needs but few resources? It wasn’t the obvious choice. But it felt right.
She threw herself into education reform, children’s advocacy, and legal aid. The work was tough, and there were plenty of obstacles. But with every small win—a child finding a safe home, a school policy finally changing—her belief in change grew stronger. Even when the odds were stacked against her.
Marriage brought its own mix of challenges and joys. Balancing two demanding careers meant constant negotiation. There were tense moments, when ambitions clashed or when the spotlight made private moments anything but private. But there was also laughter, shared purpose, and this sense that together, they could handle just about anything. Their partnership became a real source of strength—a reminder that even in the rough patches, moving forward was always possible.
As time went on, the call to public service got louder. The idea of running for office, of stepping straight into the public eye, stopped feeling so far-fetched. Sure, it was a leap into the unknown. But it was also a chance to really put her values into action.
Her journey—from law student to advocate, partner to public figure—was full of challenges and growth. Through it all, her belief in service, something that started in childhood and was tested so many times in adulthood, stayed at the heart of everything she did.
